title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LIV
paragraphs:
“Negli occhi porta la mia donna Amore;
Per che si fa gentil ciò ch’ella mira:
Ov’ella passa, ogni uom ver lei si gira,
E cui saluta fa tremar lo core.
Sicchè, bassando il viso, tutto smore, E d’ogni suo difetto allor sospira: Fuggon dinanzi a lei Superbia ed Ira: Aiutatemi, donne, a farle onore.

Ogni dolcezza, ogni pensiero umile Nasce nel core a chi parlar la sente; Ond’è beato chi prima la vide. Quel ch’ella par quand’ un poco sorride, Non si può dicer, nè tener a mente, Si è nuovo miracolo gentile.” —DANTE: _La Vita Nuova_.

By that lovely morning when the Stone Court hayricks perfumed the air impartially, as though Mr. Raffles deserved the finest incense, Dorothea was living at Lowick Manor again. After three months, Freshitt had begun to feel oppressive. She could not spend hours every day posing like Saint Catherine, gazing ecstatically at Celia's baby. Yet a childless sister could hardly be allowed to remain in that momentous infant's presence while persistently ignoring him. Had there been a need, Dorothea would gladly have carried the baby a mile, loving him all the more tenderly for the effort. But an aunt who does not recognize her nephew as Buddha, and has nothing to do for him but admire him, is liable to find his behaviour repetitive and the pleasure of watching it exhaustible. Celia could not conceive of this. To her, Dorothea's childless widowhood fitted very prettily with little Arthur's birth—the baby had been named after Mr. Brooke.

“Dodo is just the sort of person who doesn't mind having nothing of her own—children or anything!” Celia told her husband. “And if she'd had a baby, it could never have been as sweet as Arthur. Could it, James?”
“Not if it resembled Casaubon,” Sir James answered. He knew he was answering indirectly, and kept strictly to himself his actual opinion of his firstborn's perfections.

“No! Just imagine! Really, it was a mercy,” said Celia. “I think being a widow is very nice for Dodo. She can love our baby as much as if he were hers, and have as many ideas of her own as she pleases.”
“It's a pity she wasn't a queen,” said the devoted Sir James.
“But then what would we have been? We'd have had to be something different,” Celia objected, disliking such a laborious effort of imagination. “I prefer her as she is.”

So when Celia discovered that Dorothea was arranging to return permanently to Lowick, her eyebrows rose in disappointment. In her quiet, unassuming manner, she launched a needle-sharp barb of sarcasm.

“What will you do at Lowick, Dodo? You say yourself there's nothing to do. Everyone is so clean and comfortable that it makes you positively melancholy. And you've been so happy here, going round all the worst backyards in Tipton with Mr. Garth. Now uncle's abroad, the two of you can do exactly as you please. And I'm sure James does everything you tell him.”
“I'll visit often, and I'll notice baby's growth all the better,” Dorothea replied.
“But you'll never see him being washed,” said Celia. “That's the best part of the day.” She was almost pouting. It seemed cruel of Dodo to leave the baby when she could stay.

“Dear Kitty, I'll come and spend the night especially,” said Dorothea. “But just now I want to be alone in my own home. I want to know the Farebrothers better, and talk to Mr. Farebrother about what can be done in Middlemarch.”

Dorothea's natural strength of will was no longer entirely channelled into determined submission. She longed to be at Lowick and had simply decided to go. She did not feel obliged to explain every reason. Everyone around her disapproved, however. Sir James was deeply distressed. He proposed that they should all move to Cheltenham for a few months, taking the sacred ark, otherwise known as a cradle. In those days, once Cheltenham had been rejected, a man scarcely knew what else to suggest.

The Dowager Lady Chettam had just returned from visiting her daughter in London. She wanted them at least to write to Mrs. Vigo and offer her the position of companion to Mrs. Casaubon. Surely a young widow like Dorothea could not mean to live alone at Lowick. Mrs. Vigo had served royal personages as reader and secretary. Even Dorothea could find no fault with her knowledge and principles.

Mrs. Cadwallader told her privately, “You'll certainly go mad alone in that house, my dear. You'll start seeing visions. We all have to make some effort to stay sane, and to call things by the names other people use. Of course, for younger sons and penniless women, madness is one way of being provided for: somebody looks after them then. But you mustn't resort to that. I dare say our good dowager bores you a little here. Still, think what a bore you might become to everyone else if you were always playing the tragic queen and treating everything sublimely. Sitting alone in that library, you might imagine you controlled the weather. You need a few people around who wouldn't believe you if you said so. That's a good medicine for bringing one down to earth.”
“I've never called everything by the same names as the people around me,” Dorothea said firmly.
“But I assume you've discovered your mistake, my dear,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied. “Which proves you're sane.”

Dorothea recognized the sting, but it did not wound her. “No,” she said. “I still believe most people are wrong about a great many things. Surely it's possible to be sane and believe that. After all, the greater part of the world has often had to change its opinion.”

Mrs. Cadwallader pursued the point no further with Dorothea, but told her husband, “It would be best if she married again as soon as decency permits, provided we could put her among the right people. Naturally the Chettams wouldn't like that. But plainly a husband is the best way to keep her in order. If we weren't so poor, I'd invite Lord Triton. He'll be a marquis one day, and there's no denying she'd make a fine marchioness. Mourning makes her look handsomer than ever.”
“My dear Elinor, leave the poor woman alone. These schemes do no good,” said the easygoing Rector.

“No good? How else do marriages happen, except by bringing men and women together? It's a disgrace that her uncle has run off and closed the Grange just now. Plenty of eligible men ought to be invited there and to Freshitt. Lord Triton is exactly right—full of rather muddle-headed plans to make people happy. He'd suit Mrs. Casaubon perfectly.”
“Let her make her own choice, Elinor.”

“That's the nonsense you wise men talk! How can she choose without a selection to choose from? A woman's choice generally means taking the only man available. Mark my words, Humphrey. Unless her friends make an effort, we'll have something worse than the Casaubon affair.”
“For heaven's sake, don't raise that subject, Elinor! It's extremely painful to Sir James. He'd be deeply offended if you mentioned it to him unnecessarily.”
“I haven't raised it,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, spreading her hands. “Celia told me everything about the will at the very beginning, without my asking.”
“Yes, yes. But they want it kept quiet. And I understand the young man is leaving the neighbourhood.”
Mrs. Cadwallader made no answer. She merely gave her husband three meaningful nods, her dark eyes filled with sarcasm.

Despite protests and persuasion, Dorothea quietly held to her decision. By the end of June all Lowick Manor's shutters stood open. Morning looked calmly into the library, lighting the rows of notebooks as it lights a desolate waste planted with enormous stones, the silent memorial of a forgotten faith. Evening, heavy with the scent of roses, entered the blue-green sitting room where Dorothea most often chose to sit. At first she went through every room, questioning the eighteen months of her marriage and continuing her thoughts as though speaking for her husband to hear. Then she lingered in the library. She could not rest until she had carefully arranged all the notebooks in the orderly sequence she imagined he would have wanted. The pity that had restrained and compelled her during their life together still clung to his image, even as she argued with him indignantly in her thoughts and told him he had been unjust. One small act may perhaps be smiled at as superstitious. She carefully enclosed and sealed the Synoptical Tabulation for the use of Mrs. Casaubon, writing inside the envelope: “I could not use it. Do you not see now that I could not submit my soul to yours by working without hope at something I do not believe in?—Dorothea.” Then she put the paper away in her own desk.

Perhaps that silent conversation was all the more earnest because beneath it, and running through it, lay the deep longing that had truly brought her back to Lowick. She wanted to see Will Ladislaw. She could imagine no good that a meeting would do. She was helpless; her hands were tied, preventing her from redressing any unfairness in his circumstances. Yet her soul thirsted for the sight of him. How could it be otherwise? Suppose, in the days of enchantment, a princess had seen some four-footed herd animal approach her repeatedly with a human gaze, singling her out in appeal. What would occupy her thoughts as she travelled? What would she seek when herds passed by? Surely the gaze that had found her, which she would recognize again. Life would be no better than tinsel by candlelight and rubbish by day if past experience did not move our spirits to longing and constancy. Dorothea truly did want to know the Farebrothers better, and especially to speak with the new Rector. But she also remembered Lydgate's account of Will and little Miss Noble, and counted on Will visiting the family at Lowick. On the first Sunday, _before_ entering the church, she saw him exactly where he had been on her previous visit, alone in the clergyman's pew. But _when_ she went inside, he had disappeared.
During weekday visits to the Rectory ladies, she listened in vain for some passing mention of Will. Mrs. Farebrother seemed to discuss everyone else, both within the neighbourhood and beyond it.

“I suppose some of Mr. Farebrother's Middlemarch congregation may come to hear him at Lowick occasionally. Don't you think so?” Dorothea asked, rather despising herself for the question's hidden motive.

“If they have any wisdom, they will, Mrs. Casaubon,” the old lady replied. “I see you properly appreciate my son's preaching. His grandfather on my side was an excellent clergyman. His father followed the law—an exemplary and honest man nevertheless, which explains why we never became rich. They call Fortune a woman, and a capricious one. But sometimes she's a good woman who gives to the deserving. That's what you've done, Mrs. Casaubon, by giving my son a living.”

Mrs. Farebrother returned to her knitting, dignifiedly satisfied with her neat little speech. But this was not what Dorothea had hoped to hear. Poor thing! She did not even know if Will Ladislaw was still in Middlemarch. There was nobody she dared ask, except perhaps Lydgate. Just now, however, seeing him would mean sending for him or going to find him. Perhaps Will had heard of Mr. Casaubon's strange prohibition against him and decided they had better never meet again. Perhaps she was wrong to want a meeting against which others might have many sound arguments. Yet after these sensible reflections, “But I do wish it” came as naturally as a sob after holding one's breath. The meeting did happen, though in a formal manner she had not expected.

One morning at about eleven, Dorothea sat in her private sitting room with a map of the manor's lands and other papers before her. She meant to use them to make an exact account of her income and affairs. She had not begun. Her hands lay folded in her lap while she looked along the lime avenue towards the distant fields. Every sunlit leaf was still. The familiar, unchanging view seemed an image of her future: a life of purposeless comfort—purposeless unless her own energy could discover reasons for passionate action. A widow's cap in those days framed the face in an oval, its crown rising above it; her dress demonstrated how much crape could possibly be applied. Yet this heavy solemnity of clothing only made her face look younger, with its restored colour and the sweet, questioning openness of her eyes.
Tantripp interrupted her thoughts. Mr. Ladislaw was downstairs, she said, requesting permission to see Madam if it was not too early.
“I'll see him,” Dorothea said, getting up at once. “Show him into the drawing room.”

For Dorothea, the drawing room was the house's most neutral space, least connected with the trials of her marriage. The damask matched the white-and-gold woodwork. Two tall mirrors stood there, and tables with nothing on them. In short, it was a room that gave you no reason to choose one seat over another. Beneath the sitting room, it too had a bow window overlooking the avenue. When Pratt showed Will in, however, the window was open. A winged visitor buzzed in and out occasionally, indifferent to the furniture, making the room seem less formal and deserted.
“It's good to see you here again, sir,” said Pratt, lingering to adjust a blind.
“I've only come to say goodbye, Pratt,” Will replied. Even the butler should know he was too proud to linger around Mrs. Casaubon now she was a wealthy widow.

“I'm very sorry to hear that, sir,” said Pratt as he withdrew. Naturally, being a servant who must be told nothing, he knew the fact still hidden from Ladislaw and had drawn his own conclusions. He had not disagreed with his fiancée Tantripp when she said, “Your master was jealous as a fiend, without any cause. Madam would look higher than Mr. Ladislaw, or I don't know her. Mrs. Cadwallader's maid says there's a lord coming to marry her when the mourning's over.”

Will had only a few moments to pace the room with his hat in his hand before Dorothea appeared. How different this was from their first meeting in Rome, when he had been embarrassed and she composed. Now he was miserable but determined, while her agitation could not be concealed. Just outside the door she had felt that this longed-for meeting was, after all, too difficult. As Will approached, a deep blush, rare for her, came with painful suddenness. Neither knew why, but neither spoke. She briefly offered her hand, then they sat near the window on facing settees. Will felt particularly uncomfortable. It seemed unlike Dorothea to receive him so differently merely because she was now a widow. He knew of no other change that could have affected their former relationship—except, as his imagination immediately suggested, that her friends might have been poisoning her mind with their suspicions.
“I hope I haven't presumed by calling,” Will said. “I couldn't bear to leave the neighbourhood and begin a new life without seeing you to say goodbye.”

“Presumed? Certainly not. I'd have thought it unkind if you hadn't wanted to see me,” said Dorothea. Her habit of complete sincerity asserted itself through all her uncertainty and distress. “Are you leaving straight away?”

“Very soon, I think. I mean to go to London and qualify for the bar by attending the required dinners. They say that's the preparation for every kind of public business. There'll soon be a great deal of political work, and I intend to try my hand at it. Other men have earned honourable positions without family influence or money.”

“That will only make it more honourable,” Dorothea said eagerly. “Besides, you have so many talents. My uncle has told me how well you speak in public—everyone's sorry when you finish—and how clearly you explain things. And you want justice for everyone. I'm so glad. In Rome I thought you cared only about poetry and art, the things that embellish life for those of us who are comfortably off. Now I know you think about everyone else as well.”
As she spoke, Dorothea's personal embarrassment faded. She became her former self again, looking straight at Will with delighted confidence.

“So you approve of my going away for years, and never returning until I've made some mark in the world?” Will asked. He was struggling to reconcile the utmost pride with an equally strong effort to draw some expression of deep feeling from her.

She did not realize how long she took to answer. Turning her head, she looked through the window at the rosebushes. They seemed to contain all the summers of the years Will would be gone. This was not prudent behaviour. But Dorothea never thought of calculating her manner; she thought only of submitting to the sad necessity that separated them. His first words about his plans had seemed to explain everything. She assumed he knew all about Mr. Casaubon's final action concerning him, and that the discovery had shocked him as it had shocked her. He had only ever felt friendship for her. Nothing in his mind had justified what she considered her husband's outrage against both their feelings. Yet his friendship remained. Something like a silent inward sob passed through Dorothea before she spoke. Her clear voice trembled at the last words, almost as though only from its own fluid flexibility.
“Yes, what you propose must be right. I'll be very happy to hear that people have recognized your worth. But you'll need patience. It may take a long time.”

Will could never quite explain how he stopped himself falling at her feet when she spoke that gently trembling “long time.” Afterwards he used to say that the dreadful colour and texture of her crape dress had probably restrained him. He remained seated, however, and said only—
“I'll never hear from you. And you'll forget me entirely.”

“No,” Dorothea replied, “I won't forget you. I've never forgotten anyone I once knew. My life has never been crowded, and I don't expect it will be. Besides, there's plenty of room for memories at Lowick, isn't there?” She smiled.

“Good God!” Will exclaimed passionately. Still holding his hat, he rose and walked to a marble table, suddenly turning to lean his back against it. Colour flooded his face and neck; he looked almost angry. He felt as though they were two creatures slowly turning into marble before one another, their hearts still conscious and their eyes still longing. But nothing could be done. He would never allow it to be said that he had come to this meeting with bitter determination only to end by confessing feelings that could be interpreted as a request for her fortune. Moreover, he really feared the effect such a confession might have on Dorothea herself.

From across the room she watched him uneasily, wondering if her words had offended him. Meanwhile her thoughts kept returning to his probable lack of money and her inability to help. Had her uncle been home, she might have done something through him! Her preoccupation with the hardship of Will's poverty, while she possessed what should have been his share, led her to speak again as he remained silent, looking away.
“I wonder whether you'd like the miniature hanging upstairs—I mean that lovely portrait of your grandmother. If you'd like it, I don't think I ought to keep it. It looks remarkably like you.”
“That's very kind,” Will said irritably. “No, I don't particularly want it. Owning one's own likeness isn't much consolation. It would be more comforting if someone else wanted it.”
“I thought you'd want to cherish her memory. I thought—” Dorothea stopped briefly, her imagination warning her away from Aunt Julia's history. “Surely you'd like the miniature as a family keepsake.”
“Why should I have that when I've nothing else? A man whose only storage is a portmanteau has to keep his memories in his head.”

Will spoke without thinking, simply releasing his irritation. Being offered his grandmother's portrait at that moment was a little too exasperating. But Dorothea found a particular sting in his words. She stood and answered with a trace of both indignation and pride.
“Having nothing makes you much the happier of the two of us, Mr. Ladislaw.”

Will was taken aback. Whatever she meant, her tone sounded like a dismissal. He stopped leaning against the table and moved a little towards her. Their eyes met with a strange, questioning seriousness. Something kept their minds apart, leaving each to guess the other's thoughts. Will had never really considered himself entitled to inherit any of the property Dorothea now held. He would have needed the whole story explained to understand what she was feeling.
“Until now, I've never thought having nothing a misfortune,” he said. “But poverty can be as bad as leprosy if it separates us from what we care for most.”
The words pierced Dorothea's heart and softened her. She answered with the sadness of someone who understood.

“Sorrow reaches us in so many ways. Two years ago I didn't understand that—the unexpected ways trouble comes, tying our hands and silencing us when we're longing to speak. I used to feel rather contemptuous of women for not shaping their lives more, for not doing better things. I was very fond of having my own way. I've almost given that up,” she finished with a playful smile.

“I haven't given up doing what I want, but I very rarely can,” said Will. He stood two yards away, his mind crowded with conflicting wishes and resolutions. He longed for unmistakable proof that she loved him, yet dreaded the position such proof might put him in. “What we want most may come with conditions we couldn't possibly bear.”
Just then Pratt came in. “Sir James Chettam is in the library, madam.”

“Ask him to come here,” Dorothea said at once. It was as though one electric shock had passed through both her and Will. Each felt a proud defiance. Neither looked at the other as they waited for Sir James.
After shaking Dorothea's hand, Sir James gave Ladislaw the slightest possible bow. Will returned it with precisely equal coldness. Then he approached Dorothea and said—
“I must say goodbye, Mrs. Casaubon. Probably for a long time.”

Dorothea held out her hand and said goodbye warmly. Sensing that Sir James was treating Will as an inferior and behaving rudely, she felt her resolution and dignity rise. There was no embarrassment in her manner. After Will left, she turned to Sir James with such calm composure and asked, “How is Celia?” that he had to act as though nothing had displeased him. What would any other behaviour achieve? Indeed, Sir James disliked so intensely even the thought of Dorothea and Ladislaw as possible lovers that he wished to avoid any display of irritation acknowledging the possibility. Asked why he recoiled so strongly, he might at first have offered nothing fuller or more precise than “_That_ Ladislaw!” On reflection, he might have argued that Mr. Casaubon's codicil, penalizing a marriage between them, made any relationship whatsoever inappropriate. His aversion grew stronger because he felt powerless to intervene.
Yet Sir James exerted an influence he never suspected. By arriving at that moment, he embodied the strongest reasons that made Will's pride a force of resistance, holding him apart from Dorothea.
